title: Stealing minds
hookLine: deceiving someone, even without taking money

cards: A friend is passing your door. You call out: come in, stay for dinner! You say it warmly, and you know for certain that he can't; he's on his way somewhere and will say no.
He leaves feeling cared for. You leave looking generous. Nothing was taken from him.
No coin, no object, nothing anyone could report. And yet the Talmud uses this exact scene as an example of stealing. What could have been stolen?

teach.b: Literally, the stealing of knowledge, or of the mind: creating a false impression in someone, getting credit or goodwill you didn't earn. First, the rule.

In tractate Chullin, the sage Shmuel says it is forbidden to steal the mind of any person, and adds that this includes a person who isn't Jewish. The rule isn't about one's own community. It's about every mind.
Second, the examples, all small and domestic. Don't press a friend to eat with you when you know he won't. Don't load him with gifts you know he'll refuse.
Don't open a barrel of wine and let him think it's in his honor, when you were opening it to sell anyway.
Every example is a kindness that isn't real. Third, a story you met in year three. In the Second Book of Samuel, David's son Absalom stands by the city gate.
Whoever comes with a case, he greets, kisses, and tells: if only I were judge, you'd get justice.
The verse sums it up: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." He took nothing from their purses. He took their trust, and used it to turn them against his father.
Money stolen can be paid back. A false picture planted in someone's head keeps working after you've gone: they decide, trust, vote and buy on what you let them believe.
The tradition treats a person's understanding as their own. Mislead it, and you've reached in and taken something.

how: Jewish law codes treat genevat da'at as a prohibition in its own right, and it's discussed in contexts from shopkeeping and advertising to everyday social courtesies.

o: taking goods from a shop when no one is watching
forgetting what you learned by never reviewing it
creating a false impression, even with no money taken

p: opened to sell, not to honor
stole the hearts of the men of Israel

s: genevat da'at only counts if money is lost
it means creating a false impression, even when nothing is taken.
Shmuel's rule covers deceiving people who aren't Jewish too
in tractate Chullin he says it is forbidden to steal the mind of any person, including a non-Jew.
the Talmud's examples are all about big business fraud
they're small and domestic: an invitation you know will be refused, gifts, a barrel of wine.

games.q: you're opening a barrel of wine to sell. a friend walks in. what does the Talmud say not to do?
o: let him think you opened it in his honor.
games.why: letting him think it's in his honor is the example the Talmud gives. a kindness that isn't real is a kind of theft.

practice: Look ahead at today's conversations one by one: the email, the meeting, the sale, the dinner, the photo you might post.
Is there a place where you're tempted to let someone believe something that isn't so, an offer you don't mean, a busyness you're exaggerating, a compliment given to get something back?
Find one, and decide now what the plain version sounds like.

wordCard.voice: Genevat da'at. The stealing of the mind: deceiving someone, even when no money is taken. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: stealing of the mind, of knowledge.

carryVoice: Your line: don't steal minds. A kindness only counts when it's real. Another step up the hill.

sources.q: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel
